methodological_rigor.justification: The CCGA3 cohort follow-up (n=2,513 with stageable invasive cancer) is large and multicenter, with explicit inclusion/exclusion (plasma cell neoplasms, nonstaged, and multiple primaries excluded) and clear censoring from blood draw to death or last-known-alive. The analytical strategy of comparing observed survival to a SEER-matched expected survival (matched on age, sex, cancer type, and stage) using one-sample proportional-hazards tests and MCMC-based between-group HR estimation is appropriate for handling heterogeneity across cancer types/stages that would confound a naive CSD vs NCSD comparison, and the Discussion explicitly concedes limitations: healthy-volunteer bias, OS rather than cancer-specific mortality, absence of treatment and smoking data, no matching on histologic subtype, and that HRs may be suboptimal given time-varying hazards. Weaknesses include no reported power calculation, no sensitivity analyses around the 1.5% lost-to-follow-up or informative censoring, no competing-risks framework, no multiplicity correction across stage-stratified tests, and no verification of proportional-hazards assumptions. Statistically, methods are generally sound with CIs and p-values reported and a thoughtful reference-population framework, but pre-specification of the analysis plan is not clearly stated.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual prospective cohort analysis nested within a case-control test-development study (CCGA3) with 5-year longitudinal follow-up, classifying as Oxford 2b for prognostic evidence. The clinical question of whether MCED-detected early-stage cancers represent overdiagnosed indolent disease or micrometastatic lethal cancers is of direct, high-stakes relevance to population screening policy and ongoing MCED regulatory and reimbursement debates. Endpoints are patient-centered overall survival at a 5-year landmark, and the finding that early-stage CSD cancers have survival comparable to SEER-matched conventionally diagnosed cases directly addresses a central mechanistic objection to MCED screening. The paper does not provide interventional screening-outcome evidence (OS benefit from randomization to screening), which caps clinical actionability below 5.

reporting_quality.justification: REMARK is the most applicable checklist because the manuscript evaluates a biomarker (MCED test result) for prognostic significance; STROBE could also apply as a secondary observational-reporting lens. The report covers most key REMARK items: assay description (methylation sequencing, blinded to clinicians), participant source and timing (142 sites, Aug 2016–Feb 2019), inclusion/exclusion, follow-up strategy, participant flow (Fig 1), stratified analyses, and candid limitations including unmeasured covariates and histologic subtypes. Gaps include no explicit statement of prespecification/analysis plan for this 5-year follow-up, no sample-size justification, limited reporting of handling of missing covariates, and reliance on prior publications for assay performance details. Data/code availability is weak as presented: no mention of a public data repository, no code deposit for the SEER-matching or Stan/RStan pipeline, and SEER access is public but the derived matched reference datasets and model code are not shared in the manuscript text (acknowledging blinding may have removed a data-availability statement).

novelty_literature.justification: The work is a meaningful but incremental extension of a prior CCGA2 analysis (reference 21, Chen et al. 2021) that already established the prognostic value of CSD vs NCSD with 3-year follow-up; this update uses the refined (CCGA3) test, extends follow-up to 5 years, and introduces a SEER-matched expected-survival framework with MCMC-based between-group HR estimation. Empirical novelty lies chiefly in showing that early-stage CSD cancers do not have excess mortality relative to SEER-matched conventionally diagnosed cases, which directly engages the overdiagnosis-vs-micrometastasis debate for MCED screening. The analytical approach of one-sample proportional-hazards against a SEER-derived expected curve is adapted from existing methods (Finkelstein et al.), not newly developed. Conceptual and methodological novelty are modest, and comparable prognostic analyses from the same program and related ctDNA-shedding literature already exist.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized with a well-scoped Introduction that motivates the overdiagnosis vs micrometastasis question, Methods that cleanly separate design and statistics, and Results that use descriptive subheads to guide the reader. The Abstract is quantitatively grounded and faithful to the body (CSD vs NCSD death rates 85% vs 34%; observed vs expected 5-year survival 43% vs 40% CSD, 88% vs 81% NCSD). Figure captions are informative and standalone, acronyms are generally expanded on first use, and the Discussion engages mechanistic alternatives and limitations in a balanced way. Minor issues: some repetition between Results narrative and figure captions, and the Discussion rehashes several numbers already reported in the Results.

key_strengths: Large (n=2,513), multicenter prospective cohort with 5-year landmark follow-up and only 1.5% loss to follow-up
SEER-matched expected-survival framework (matched on age, sex, cancer type, stage) appropriately handles between-group heterogeneity that would otherwise confound CSD vs NCSD comparison
Directly addresses the clinically important overdiagnosis-vs-micrometastasis critique of MCED screening with patient-centered OS endpoints
Transparent, well-structured limitations section covering healthy-volunteer bias, OS vs cause-specific mortality, missing treatment/smoking data, and histologic subtype confounding
Clear, quantitatively faithful abstract and informative figure captions
key_concerns: No power calculation, no verification of proportional-hazards assumption, and no multiplicity correction across stage-stratified tests
Residual confounding from unmatched histologic subtypes (notably indolent prostate/breast) likely inflates NCSD survival advantage, as the authors themselves acknowledge
OS without competing-risks or cancer-specific mortality limits causal attribution of the prognostic signal to MCED detection
Novelty is incremental over the prior CCGA2 3-year analysis (ref 21); the test version and follow-up window are updated but the core finding and framework are extensions
Data and analysis code (SEER-matching pipeline, Stan models) are not clearly deposited, limiting independent replication
Prespecification of the 5-year analysis plan is not explicitly documented
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically solid prognostic cohort analysis with clear translational relevance to MCED screening policy, but incremental over prior CCGA work and lacking several rigor elements (prespecification, competing risks, code sharing); fits Tier 2 oncology venues with minor revisions.
